items.content_excerpt: $BTC.X $NVDA AI Bubble and Bitcoin Arthur Hayes is warning of a potential AI bubble. Trillions are being invested worldwide in data centers, energy and computing power, while many AI companies still struggle to make these massive investments profitable. According to Hayes, the bill could come due in late 2027 or 2028: too much capacity, too much debt, and eventually a crash. That could then trigger another bailout, with huge amounts of liquidity flowing back into the financial system. And that’s where it gets interesting for crypto. Bitcoin could absorb part of that excess liquidity, according to Hayes. A crisis could initially cause a sharp sell-off, but if governments and central banks respond with renewed monetary easing, that liquidity could eventually become fuel for Bitcoin and crypto. The irony? Maybe the problem won’t be AI itself, but the enormous financial bubble surrounding it. And if AI does succeed, projects focused on AI, compute and decentralized infrastructure.

It's legal, it's disclosed, and it's compliant with independent audit oversight. 2. The Escalation: Once a CEO realizes they can seamlessly slide $900 million from a private entity into a public entity's revenue column to satisfy Wall Street, the temptation to repeat that trick to cover up a bad quarter becomes irresistible. 3. The Result: The reported financials stop reflecting true consumer demand in the open market and start reflecting internal financial engineering. items.title: Wells Fargo analyst Ken Gawrelski raised his price target on Meta Platforms to $1,000 from $796, making it the highest target among analysts
items.content_excerpt: Wells Fargo analyst Ken Gawrelski raised his price target on Meta Platforms to $1,000 from $796, making it the highest target among analysts tracked by FactSet. The upgrade reflects expectations that Meta’s artificial-intelligence investments, including its Muse AI assistant, can drive substantial earnings growth despite near-term pressure on profits. Gawrelski expects Meta’s third-quarter EPS to fall to $3.72, partly due to an anticipated $10 billion legal-settlement charge. The company is also facing higher AI infrastructure spending, which could weigh on profitability in the near term. However, Wells Fargo believes these costs are positioning Meta for much stronger growth through 2028. The firm sees the combination of AI monetization, improving infrastructure efficiency and continued growth across Meta’s advertising ecosystem as potential catalysts for a major expansion in earnings and valuation. $META

items.content_excerpt: ERock shares jumped 10.09% Tuesday as investors focused on the company’s exposure to the rapidly growing power needs of artificial-intelligence data centers. The company makes modular, natural-gas-fired power units that can provide electricity directly to AI data centers, positioning it as a potential beneficiary of the surge in AI infrastructure spending. The move highlights a broader investment theme: the enormous electricity requirements of AI computing are creating new opportunities for companies involved in power generation and data-center infrastructure. As hyperscalers and technology companies expand AI capacity, reliable and quickly deployable power has become increasingly important, particularly in regions where grid connections can take years. ERock’s modular RockBlock generators are designed to address that challenge by providing scalable on-site power generation. $EROC $CEG $GOOGL $META

items.title: Google is making another major bet on nuclear power as the rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence data centers intensifies the need for
items.content_excerpt: Google is making another major bet on nuclear power as the rapid expansion of artificial-intelligence data centers intensifies the need for reliable electricity. The company announced Tuesday a new long-term agreement with Constellation Energy covering 890 megawatts of nuclear capacity from existing facilities in Illinois. The companies said the contracted power is roughly equivalent to the output of a new nuclear reactor. The deal highlights the growing importance of nuclear energy for major AI companies facing soaring electricity requirements from data centers. Google and other technology firms are increasingly turning to nuclear power to secure dependable, low-carbon energy as AI infrastructure expands. The agreement adds to a broader push by technology companies to lock in long-term power supplies and reduce the risk that electricity constraints could limit the expansion of AI infrastructure. $CEG $GOOG $GOOGL

items.title: Waymo has significantly expanded its first private debt offering to $5 billion, capitalizing on strong lender demand as Alphabet’s autonomou
items.content_excerpt: Waymo has significantly expanded its first private debt offering to $5 billion, capitalizing on strong lender demand as Alphabet’s autonomous-driving unit accelerates capital-intensive expansion in the U.S. and internationally. According to Bloomberg, Waymo secured commitments from major private-credit investors including Pacific Investment Management Co., Blackstone and Sixth Street Partners. The loan was arranged with Goldman Sachs and priced at 5.25 percentage points above the benchmark rate. The expanded debt facility marks a shift from Waymo’s previous reliance on equity financing. Earlier this year, the company raised $16 billion at a $126 billion valuation to fund autonomous-vehicle initiatives and hardware development, including custom chips for its fleet. The new financing comes as Waymo faces rising AI and fleet-acquisition costs while expanding across the U.S. and preparing for entry into major Asian markets such as Japan and Singapore. $GOOGL $BX $GS

items.content_excerpt: $ORCL This is bullish for $ORCL in more ways than one. Paramount/Skydance is already an Oracle Cloud customer under a 6-year, $300M OCI agreement. Now the $111B Warner deal has officially closed, creating a media giant spanning Warner Bros., HBO/HBO Max, CNN, CBS, Paramount+ and more than 200M streaming subscribers. That creates enormous potential demand for cloud infrastructure, streaming, data and AI — and OCI is already inside the door. But there’s another important angle: Larry Ellison personally backed his son David’s bid with a massive financial guarantee. With the deal now successfully closed, a major source of uncertainty and potential financial exposure hanging over Larry has been substantially reduced. So this is potentially a double win for $ORCL: More potential OCI business from a vastly larger Skydance — and significantly less deal-related financial risk for Oracle’s largest individual shareholder. The $300M OCI contract may only be the beginning. $PLTR

items.title: $SOFI people are so irrationally obsessed with this stock. The issue with this stock is very simple: the earnings per share just aren’t ther
items.content_excerpt: $SOFI people are so irrationally obsessed with this stock. The issue with this stock is very simple: the earnings per share just aren’t there. The EPS remains too low. Trailing is under 50 cents. Forward earnings of $1.00 per share aren’t due for a while (not the next 12 months, for example, which look more like 73 cents). And, it’s a bank, a consumer lending institution. The “tech platform” side didn’t pan out. Banks don’t sell at 30x or 40x. Just go look at other banks. And they don’t sell at more than 3x tangible book value either. As to *why* the EPS hasn’t grown more, partly it’s the dilution, and partly the disappointment from the tech side of the business. The core business of making loans and selling off the portfolios is what it is, they could easily have gone more in the Robinhood direction, but they had a very different vision (and a very different CEO). So, I don’t see why anyone thinks it’s worth much more than $16 today.

items.title: $USO $SPY U.S. President Donald Trump isn’t “completely wrong” in suggesting that the disruption to energy flows via the Strait of Hormuz is
items.content_excerpt: $USO $SPY U.S. President Donald Trump isn’t “completely wrong” in suggesting that the disruption to energy flows via the Strait of Hormuz is Asia’s problem, Singapore Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan said. Asian economies are among the biggest customers of energy shipped through the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow waterway connecting the Persian Gulf with the Arabian Sea, making any prolonged disruption particularly consequential for the region. Balakrishnan, however, cautioned against viewing the issue simply through the lens of who buys the oil, stressing the importance of maintaining freedom of navigation through international waterways. For Singapore, that principle is “non-negotiable,” Balakrishnan said, citing the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea and the rights of transit passage and freedom of navigation. “This, for us, is an existential question, and it’s a matter of principle, matter of international law,” Balakrishnan said. https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/07/hormuz-iran-war-singapore-vivian-balakrishnan.html

items.content_excerpt: $QQQ The Nasdaq closed at a record for the second straight day. The S&P set one too, closing above 7,800 for the first time, its 28th record of the year. The odd part is who led: utilities. Since 1990, the S&P has set a first record after a 30+ day drought 61 times. Utilities led only twice before today (Dow Jones Market Data). That is the power leg of the AI trade doing the lifting. Constellation Energy closed up 12.3% on the Alphabet deal, Vistra ran with it, Nvidia set its own second straight record close. The Dow is still about 5% below its August record. And all of this landed with the 10-year at 5.27%, a hair below a 24-year high. Glenmede's Jason Pride called it a broad sentiment read on the rally's strength, while admitting there was no clear fundamental catalyst for the day.

items.content_excerpt: $NLST We have now achieved settlements with Samsung and MU! That has moved the SP from below $1 to $6.66 yesterday. The next two steps should have a similar combined effect in terms of additional dollars: first, a new SK hynix deal. I expect that within the next few weeks, certainly within the current quarter, so that SK hynix is already paying fully for the next one. And then, as the second step, an announcement of a return to NASDAQ. With institutions and ETFs coming in, the P/E could double over time. Foolish to sell at the current SP. The point is: compare how difficult and how much long-term litigation was required to bring/force Samsung and Micron to settle. Now compare that with how much easier it should be to sign a new deal with SK hynix—also swimming in money—on terms similar to Samsung and Micron, and then apply for a NASDAQ listing. These latter two steps should, in my view, add at least as many dollars to the SP as the first two did: the settlements with Samsung and Micron.

items.title: $NLST Unlike any anticipated litigation outcome, an application to move from OTC to Nasdaq has a certain outcome: NASDAQ listing. And it cou
items.content_excerpt: $NLST Unlike any anticipated litigation outcome, an application to move from OTC to Nasdaq has a certain outcome: NASDAQ listing. And it could reasonably be expected to lead to a substantial P/E re-rating— doubling over some time, alone because of the relisting! If the P/E doubles, then—assuming earnings remain unchanged—the share price should roughly double as well. That would not happen in a single day. It would likely take weeks or even months, because institutions do not all buy at once. Even without SK hynix, I see no reason why Nasdaq would not welcome Netlist back, provided the formal listing requirements are met. And given that a new SK hynix deal should, in my view, not take more than a few weeks, I would expect a Nasdaq announcement soon after the new SK hynix agreement

items.content_excerpt: $CIEN Today's 13.9% move was Marvell's math, not Ciena's. At its investor day today, Marvell framed sector growth well above what Ciena told investors at its own forum on Sept 16. Marvell's read puts sector growth at 60 to 70% through 2030, versus Ciena's own roughly 30% annual revenue growth target to about 14B by fiscal 2029 (via Insider Monkey's summary; Ciena's target verified in the Sept 16 forum recap). One level down: Marvell's own 2031 split puts interconnect (37.5B) ahead of custom silicon (30B). That makes the networking plumbing the bigger leg of AI spend, which is Ciena's domain. Either Ciena's target is sandbagged or Marvell's TAM is optimistic. The tape bought the gap. Ciena closed at 443.65, up 53.96, on about 6.4M shares vs a 2M average. Tracking the forum thread into Ciena's own numbers.

items.content_excerpt: $DKNG $FLUT $PENN the October-to-January period is structurally important for online sports-betting stocks, but I’d refine your thesis. October is particularly attractive because the NFL is already underway while NBA + NHL start, creating an unusually dense sports calendar. DraftKings itself has said October is the period when all four major U.S. sports overlap and expects its busiest activity ahead. NFL → NBA → NHL → college football → NBA/NHL → NFL playoffs → Super Bowl That creates a long runway of high betting engagement rather than a one-week catalyst. The strongest fundamental case would be: higher betting handle + customer acquisition + improved hold + lower promotional intensity → higher revenue/EBITDA estimates → multiple expansion.

items.title: $VSTM My personal scorecard for October 14 I'd score it like this: 🟢 Home run ORR >40% in PDAC + strong NSCLC + meaningful CRC + clea
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM My personal scorecard for October 14 I'd score it like this: 🟢 Home run ORR >40% in PDAC + strong NSCLC + meaningful CRC + clean safety Potential stock reaction: $10 → $12–15+ 🟢 Strong 30–40% ORR PDAC + good NSCLC + emerging CRC + clean safety Potential: $10 → $11–13 🟡 Good but not spectacular 25–35% ORR + reasonable DOR + safety good Potential: $9–11 🟠 Mixed Some responses but: weak durability inconsistent tumor types questionable dose response Potential: $7–9 🔴 Bad Poor ORR + toxicity + weak durability. Potential: $5–7 Those are scenario ranges, not price targets. Here's the part that changes my opinion of VSTM When we first discussed VSTM, I viewed VS-7375 as: promising but speculative. After digging into the latest GenFleet data and the Nature Medicine publication, I'd now describe it as: clinically validated enough to be considered a serious emerging KRAS-G12D asset, but not yet validated enough to call it best-in-class. That's a meaningful upgrade.

items.title: $VSTM And now the really interesting part for VSTM shareholders GenFleet has already taken GFH375 into: Phase 3 pancreatic cancer and Phase
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM And now the really interesting part for VSTM shareholders GenFleet has already taken GFH375 into: Phase 3 pancreatic cancer and Phase 3 NSCLC. The September Nature Medicine publication also confirms the broader clinical development program and the Phase 2 expansion. So VSTM isn't inventing the development pathway. The molecule has already generated enough evidence in China for GenFleet to take it deep into development. That's a substantial de-risking factor. But there's a huge competitive elephant Revolution Medicines. Zoldonrasib has generated real data. And the broader KRAS field is moving quickly. So VSTM doesn't merely need: "Does VS-7375 work?" It needs: "Is VS-7375 good enough to compete?" That is a much higher bar. The GenFleet NSCLC data are encouraging on this point. The PDAC data are encouraging. But October is where we start getting enough U.S. data to judge this seriously.

items.title: $VSTM That's significant because NSCLC gives VSTM a second major tumor franchise. And VSTM's U.S. Phase 2 specifically includes pati
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM That's significant because NSCLC gives VSTM a second major tumor franchise. And VSTM's U.S. Phase 2 specifically includes patients with: asymptomatic untreated brain metastases. If VS-7375 demonstrates intracranial activity, that could be a major valuation catalyst. Here's what I think Wall Street will actually look for Forget management saying: "best-in-class." I don't care. I want five numbers. 1. ORR How many tumors actually shrink? 2. Confirmed ORR How many responses persist? 3. DOR How long do responders remain responders? 4. PFS Does tumor control actually translate into meaningful disease control? 5. Safety at the effective dose Can patients stay on the drug? The magic combination The dream result isn't actually 60% ORR. It's: 40% ORR 10–12+ month DOR 8–10+ month PFS clean safety. I'd rather have that than: 60% ORR 3-month DOR. That's the distinction between a drug and a potential blockbuster.

items.title: $VSTM It's saying: "We have one molecule showing activity across three major KRAS-G12D tumor types." That's a different va
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM It's saying: "We have one molecule showing activity across three major KRAS-G12D tumor types." That's a different valuation proposition. The CRC data are the wildcard I'm less confident here. VSTM's June data showed promising efficacy with full-dose cetuximab at 600 and 900 mg, but follow-up was very early. And that's why I don't assign equal probability to all three indications. My current probability estimates: Indication Probability October shows meaningful activity PDAC 80–90% NSCLC 75–85% CRC 60–75% PDAC is the strongest evidence base. NSCLC is now extremely interesting because of the GenFleet Phase 2 result. CRC is the least mature. The NSCLC result is potentially the sleeper I actually think investors may initially focus on pancreatic cancer. But look at what GenFleet just showed: 52.1% confirmed ORR in heavily pretreated KRAS-G12D NSCLC. And: 9.6-month median PFS in taxane-naïve patients.

items.title: $VSTM And that can matter enormously if investigators need to optimize exposure. Now let's talk about October 14 specifically I don'
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM And that can matter enormously if investigators need to optimize exposure. Now let's talk about October 14 specifically I don't think VSTM needs to report: 50% ORR across everything for October to be a success. That's an important distinction. I would call the readout good if we see something like: PDAC ORR around 30–40%+ with meaningful duration signals. NSCLC ORR around 35–45%+ with durable responses. CRC some convincing activity, particularly with cetuximab. Safety still manageable. If we get that: I think the market will take notice. What would make me go absolutely nuts? This is my "holy shit" scenario. Suppose October shows something approaching: PDAC 40–50% ORR NSCLC 40–50%+ ORR CRC 30%+ ORR AND: median DOR still immature AND: PFS looking durable AND: no meaningful new toxicity. That would be extremely powerful. Because then VSTM isn't just saying: "We have a KRAS G12D inhibitor that works."

items.title: $VSTM This may be almost as important as efficacy. At 600 mg and 900 mg: GI events were predominantly low grade nausea/vomiting/diarrhea gen
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM This may be almost as important as efficacy. At 600 mg and 900 mg: GI events were predominantly low grade nausea/vomiting/diarrhea generally diminished after cycle 1 very little rash no rash above Grade 1 no clinically meaningful cytopenias no clinically meaningful liver abnormalities reported in those cohorts very few grade-3 events no unexpected safety signal no meaningful cumulative toxicity identified so far One Grade 3 nausea case at 900 mg resolved in four days after antiemetic optimization. That's a very usable safety profile if it continues. And usability matters because the KRAS field is getting crowded. There's another clue I really like VSTM has already cleared: 1,200 mg QD without dose-limiting toxicities. That's above the current 900-mg dose used in the registration-directed studies. That doesn't mean 1,200 mg is better. It does mean there appears to be some pharmacologic headroom.

items.title: $VSTM But here's the evidence that really makes me comfortable Look at the PDAC biomarker. VSTM reported: 13/14 patients at 900 mg QD ha
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM But here's the evidence that really makes me comfortable Look at the PDAC biomarker. VSTM reported: 13/14 patients at 900 mg QD had: >50% reduction in CA19-9. That's 93%. Now, before anybody gets carried away: CA19-9 reduction is not equivalent to tumor response. It cannot substitute for ORR, PFS or OS. But when you see: CA19-9 falling dramatically plus actual tumor reductions plus dose-dependent activity plus GenFleet independently showing responses the biological story becomes much harder to dismiss. And I really like the dose-response signal This matters. VSTM said there was evidence of: 600 mg → 900 mg dose-dependent antitumor activity in PDAC. And the 900-mg dose achieves higher target exposure. That is exactly what you want to see. If you had: 400 works, 600 doesn't, 900 doesn't I'd worry. Instead we're seeing: more drug exposure → stronger biological activity That's encouraging pharmacology. Safety is another major positive

items.title: $VSTM Why I'm NOT giving it a 90% probability This is where I want to be careful. The Chinese data are enormously encouraging. But they
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM Why I'm NOT giving it a 90% probability This is where I want to be careful. The Chinese data are enormously encouraging. But they don't guarantee the U.S. TARGET-D 101 dataset will look identical. There are several reasons. 1. Patient populations differ The GenFleet studies were conducted primarily in China. VSTM's U.S./international population can have different: prior therapies disease burden tumor biology geographic mix treatment histories 2. Small cohorts can lie This is the classic biotech problem. A: 58% ORR in n=12 can become: 35% ORR in n=40 as the denominator grows. That's not failure. But it changes the story. 3. Follow-up matters enormously The June VSTM data were still early. In NSCLC, only one of 20+ patients at 600 mg had more than six months of follow-up at the June cutoff. In CRC, none of the 20+ patients at 600 mg had >6 months follow-up. PDAC was further along. That's why October is so important. We're finally getting more mature data.

items.title: $VSTM The idea is sustained inhibition of KRAS signaling rather than relying on only one conformational state. That's different from sev
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM The idea is sustained inhibition of KRAS signaling rather than relying on only one conformational state. That's different from several competing approaches. And the PK data from VSTM indicate the 900-mg dose achieves target plasma exposure and provides clear separation from 600 mg. That's important because early oncology programs frequently die from: great biology → inadequate exposure → disappointing clinical efficacy. VS-7375 doesn't currently look like that problem.

items.title: $VSTM Here's the really important comparison The best way to understand whether VS-7375 has a shot at being a major drug is to compare i
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM Here's the really important comparison The best way to understand whether VS-7375 has a shot at being a major drug is to compare it with other KRAS-G12D programs. One of the leaders is Revolution Medicines' zoldonrasib/RMC-9805. Its earlier Phase 1 PDAC data showed approximately: 30% ORR and: 80% DCR at the 1200-mg daily dose. VS-7375's GenFleet PDAC data have shown: 40.7% ORR overall - and: 58.3% ORR in 2L PDAC. That's why I don't think VSTM is simply another small biotech with a "promising molecule." There is a legitimate competitive efficacy signal here. And the mechanism makes sense This is another reason I am more confident. VS-7375 is designed to bind both: KRAS G12D ON and KRAS G12D OFF states.

items.title: $VSTM 🕵️‍♂️But it gets even more interesting GenFleet's newer NSCLC Phase 2 data are substantially better than the original Phase 1 data
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM 🕵️‍♂️But it gets even more interesting GenFleet's newer NSCLC Phase 2 data are substantially better than the original Phase 1 dataset. At 600 mg QD: 71 patients had at least one post-treatment assessment ... and: ORR = 59.2% confirmed ORR = 52.1% DCR = 93% That's a very serious signal in previously treated KRAS-G12D NSCLC. And the September update reported: median PFS = 9.6 months among taxane-naïve patients. The 12-month OS rate was 77% in the overall population. That is probably the single most important new piece of evidence for your question. And now look at the PDAC data This is where I think the VSTM story could become explosive. GenFleet's earlier 600-mg data showed: 2L PDAC: 58.3% ORR in 12 patients. And: 3L+ PDAC: 36.2% ORR in 47 patients. DCR was: 100% in 2L and 95.7% in 3L+. The broader 59-patient evaluable dataset showed a 40.7% ORR. These aren't tiny mouse studies. These are actual heavily pretreated humans.

items.title: $VSTM 🕵️‍♂️And there is a very important reason I'm leaning bullish. The biggest thing I found: VS-7375 already has human proof-of-conce
items.content_excerpt: $VSTM 🕵️‍♂️And there is a very important reason I'm leaning bullish. The biggest thing I found: VS-7375 already has human proof-of-concept VS-7375 is also called GFH375 by GenFleet in China. This isn't a similar drug. It's the same molecule. GenFleet's Phase 1 data were just published in Nature Medicine in September 2026. And the results are pretty damn interesting. Across 74 heavily pretreated KRAS-G12D patients: PDAC: 35.1% confirmed ORR NSCLC: 35.7% confirmed ORR PDAC median PFS: 5.5 months PDAC median OS: 9.9 months NSCLC median PFS: 5.5 months NSCLC median OS: 13.4 months recommended Phase 2 dose: 600 mg QD no DLTs in dose escalation MTD not reached There was one grade-5 treatment-related event, septic shock, which is obviously something I would not brush aside. Grade ≥3 treatment-related AEs occurred in 36.5% overall, and were more common in patients previously exposed to checkpoint inhibitors. So this isn't theoretical anymore. The drug has demonstrated reproducible human antitumor activity.

items.title: $BE One underappreciated part of Bloom’s story: water. Data centers don’t just consume enormous amounts of electricity — many cooling system
items.content_excerpt: $BE One underappreciated part of Bloom’s story: water. Data centers don’t just consume enormous amounts of electricity — many cooling systems also require significant amounts of water. Bloom’s fuel-cell systems generate electricity without the large-scale water consumption associated with traditional thermal power generation. As data centers expand into areas where water availability is becoming a constraint, power technologies with a smaller water footprint could become increasingly attractive. It’s a less-discussed potential advantage for Bloom, particularly as AI infrastructure continues expanding. The future data center power stack isn’t just about MW and $/kWh — water availability may matter too. $SPY $QQQ

A crisis could initially cause a sharp sell-off, but if governments and central banks respond with renewed monetary easing, that liquidity could eventually become fuel for Bitcoin and crypto. $TSLA Munger warned that when corporate managers start bending the rules to hit short-term targets—even if it's completely legal or approved by a board committee—it creates a slippery slope he called an incremental "moral sewer." 1. The Justification: It starts out small, like SpaceX buying a few hundred utility fleet trucks that engineers actually need. It's legal, it's disclosed, and it's compliant with independent audit oversight. 2. The Escalation: Once a CEO realizes they can seamlessly slide $900 million from a private entity into a public entity's revenue column to satisfy Wall Street, the temptation to repeat that trick to cover up a bad quarter becomes irresistible. 3. The Result: The reported financials stop reflecting true consumer demand in the open market and start reflecting internal financial engineering. Munger despised this because it robs the everyday shareholder of a transparent look at a company's real underlying health. IN THE WORLD WE CALL THAT FRAUD😈

$NLST We have now achieved settlements with Samsung and MU! That has moved the SP from below $1 to $6.66 yesterday. The next two steps should have a similar combined effect in terms of additional dollars: first, a new SK hynix deal. I expect that within the next few weeks, certainly within the current quarter, so that SK hynix is already paying fully for the next one. And then, as the second step, an announcement of a return to NASDAQ. With institutions and ETFs coming in, the P/E could double over time. Foolish to sell at the current SP. The point is: compare how difficult and how much long-term litigation was required to bring/force Samsung and Micron to settle. Now compare that with how much easier it should be to sign a new deal with SK hynix—also swimming in money—on terms similar to Samsung and Micron, and then apply for a NASDAQ listing. $NLST Unlike any anticipated litigation outcome, an application to move from OTC to Nasdaq has a certain outcome: NASDAQ listing. And it could reasonably be expected to lead to a substantial P/E re-rating— doubling over some time, alone because of the relisting! If the P/E doubles, then—assuming earnings remain unchanged—the share price should roughly double as well. That would not happen in a single day. It would likely take weeks or even months, because institutions do not all buy at once. Even without SK hynix, I see no reason why Nasdaq would not welcome Netlist back, provided the formal listing requirements are met. And given that a new SK hynix deal should, in my view, not take more than a few weeks, I would expect a Nasdaq announcement soon after the new SK hynix agreement

$VSTM Avutometinib/Defactinib Shows Activity in KRAS Wild-Type Recurrent LGSOC - October 6, 2026 Author(s) Cancer Network Staff Fact checked by: Tim Cortese, Russ Conroy https://www.cancernetwork.com/view/avutometinib-defactinib-shows-activity-in-kras-wild-type-recurrent-lgsoc
$VSTM

$VSTM My personal scorecard for October 14 I'd score it like this: 🟢 Home run ORR >40% in PDAC + strong NSCLC + meaningful CRC + clean safety Potential stock reaction: $10 → $12–15+ 🟢 Strong 30–40% ORR PDAC + good NSCLC + emerging CRC + clean safety Potential: $10 → $11–13 🟡 Good but not spectacular 25–35% ORR + reasonable DOR + safety good Potential: $9–11 🟠 Mixed Some responses but: weak durability inconsistent tumor types questionable dose response Potential: $7–9 🔴 Bad Poor ORR + toxicity + weak durability. Potential: $5–7 Those are scenario ranges, not price targets. Here's the part that changes my opinion of VSTM When we first discussed VSTM, I viewed VS-7375 as: promising but speculative. After digging into the latest GenFleet data and the Nature Medicine publication, I'd now describe it as: clinically validated enough to be considered a serious emerging KRAS-G12D asset, but not yet validated enough to call it best-in-class. That's a meaningful upgrade.

$VSTM And now the really interesting part for VSTM shareholders GenFleet has already taken GFH375 into: Phase 3 pancreatic cancer and Phase 3 NSCLC. The September Nature Medicine publication also confirms the broader clinical development program and the Phase 2 expansion. So VSTM isn't inventing the development pathway. The molecule has already generated enough evidence in China for GenFleet to take it deep into development. That's a substantial de-risking factor. But there's a huge competitive elephant Revolution Medicines. Zoldonrasib has generated real data. And the broader KRAS field is moving quickly. So VSTM doesn't merely need: "Does VS-7375 work?" It needs: "Is VS-7375 good enough to compete?" That is a much higher bar. The GenFleet NSCLC data are encouraging on this point. The PDAC data are encouraging. But October is where we start getting enough U.S. data to judge this seriously.

$VSTM That's significant because NSCLC gives VSTM a second major tumor franchise. And VSTM's U.S. Phase 2 specifically includes patients with: asymptomatic untreated brain metastases. If VS-7375 demonstrates intracranial activity, that could be a major valuation catalyst. Here's what I think Wall Street will actually look for Forget management saying: "best-in-class." I don't care. I want five numbers. 1. ORR How many tumors actually shrink? 2. Confirmed ORR How many responses persist? 3. DOR How long do responders remain responders? 4. PFS Does tumor control actually translate into meaningful disease control? 5. Safety at the effective dose Can patients stay on the drug? The magic combination The dream result isn't actually 60% ORR. It's: 40% ORR 10–12+ month DOR 8–10+ month PFS clean safety. I'd rather have that than: 60% ORR 3-month DOR. That's the distinction between a drug and a potential blockbuster.

$VSTM It's saying: "We have one molecule showing activity across three major KRAS-G12D tumor types." That's a different valuation proposition. The CRC data are the wildcard I'm less confident here. VSTM's June data showed promising efficacy with full-dose cetuximab at 600 and 900 mg, but follow-up was very early. And that's why I don't assign equal probability to all three indications. My current probability estimates: Indication Probability October shows meaningful activity PDAC 80–90% NSCLC 75–85% CRC 60–75% PDAC is the strongest evidence base. NSCLC is now extremely interesting because of the GenFleet Phase 2 result. CRC is the least mature. The NSCLC result is potentially the sleeper I actually think investors may initially focus on pancreatic cancer. But look at what GenFleet just showed: 52.1% confirmed ORR in heavily pretreated KRAS-G12D NSCLC. And: 9.6-month median PFS in taxane-naïve patients.

$VSTM And that can matter enormously if investigators need to optimize exposure. Now let's talk about October 14 specifically I don't think VSTM needs to report: 50% ORR across everything for October to be a success. That's an important distinction. I would call the readout good if we see something like: PDAC ORR around 30–40%+ with meaningful duration signals. NSCLC ORR around 35–45%+ with durable responses. CRC some convincing activity, particularly with cetuximab. Safety still manageable. If we get that: I think the market will take notice. What would make me go absolutely nuts? This is my "holy shit" scenario. Suppose October shows something approaching: PDAC 40–50% ORR NSCLC 40–50%+ ORR CRC 30%+ ORR AND: median DOR still immature AND: PFS looking durable AND: no meaningful new toxicity. That would be extremely powerful. Because then VSTM isn't just saying: "We have a KRAS G12D inhibitor that works."

$VSTM This may be almost as important as efficacy. At 600 mg and 900 mg: GI events were predominantly low grade nausea/vomiting/diarrhea generally diminished after cycle 1 very little rash no rash above Grade 1 no clinically meaningful cytopenias no clinically meaningful liver abnormalities reported in those cohorts very few grade-3 events no unexpected safety signal no meaningful cumulative toxicity identified so far One Grade 3 nausea case at 900 mg resolved in four days after antiemetic optimization. That's a very usable safety profile if it continues. And usability matters because the KRAS field is getting crowded. There's another clue I really like VSTM has already cleared: 1,200 mg QD without dose-limiting toxicities. That's above the current 900-mg dose used in the registration-directed studies. That doesn't mean 1,200 mg is better. It does mean there appears to be some pharmacologic headroom.

$VSTM But here's the evidence that really makes me comfortable Look at the PDAC biomarker. VSTM reported: 13/14 patients at 900 mg QD had: >50% reduction in CA19-9. That's 93%. Now, before anybody gets carried away: CA19-9 reduction is not equivalent to tumor response. It cannot substitute for ORR, PFS or OS. But when you see: CA19-9 falling dramatically plus actual tumor reductions plus dose-dependent activity plus GenFleet independently showing responses the biological story becomes much harder to dismiss. And I really like the dose-response signal This matters. VSTM said there was evidence of: 600 mg → 900 mg dose-dependent antitumor activity in PDAC. And the 900-mg dose achieves higher target exposure. That is exactly what you want to see. If you had: 400 works, 600 doesn't, 900 doesn't I'd worry. Instead we're seeing: more drug exposure → stronger biological activity That's encouraging pharmacology. Safety is another major positive

$VSTM Why I'm NOT giving it a 90% probability This is where I want to be careful. The Chinese data are enormously encouraging. But they don't guarantee the U.S. TARGET-D 101 dataset will look identical. There are several reasons. 1. Patient populations differ The GenFleet studies were conducted primarily in China. VSTM's U.S./international population can have different: prior therapies disease burden tumor biology geographic mix treatment histories 2. Small cohorts can lie This is the classic biotech problem. A: 58% ORR in n=12 can become: 35% ORR in n=40 as the denominator grows. That's not failure. But it changes the story. 3. Follow-up matters enormously The June VSTM data were still early. In NSCLC, only one of 20+ patients at 600 mg had more than six months of follow-up at the June cutoff. In CRC, none of the 20+ patients at 600 mg had >6 months follow-up. PDAC was further along. That's why October is so important. We're finally getting more mature data.
$VSTM

$VSTM The idea is sustained inhibition of KRAS signaling rather than relying on only one conformational state. That's different from several competing approaches. And the PK data from VSTM indicate the 900-mg dose achieves target plasma exposure and provides clear separation from 600 mg. That's important because early oncology programs frequently die from: great biology → inadequate exposure → disappointing clinical efficacy. VS-7375 doesn't currently look like that problem.

$VSTM Here's the really important comparison The best way to understand whether VS-7375 has a shot at being a major drug is to compare it with other KRAS-G12D programs. One of the leaders is Revolution Medicines' zoldonrasib/RMC-9805. Its earlier Phase 1 PDAC data showed approximately: 30% ORR and: 80% DCR at the 1200-mg daily dose. VS-7375's GenFleet PDAC data have shown: 40.7% ORR overall - and: 58.3% ORR in 2L PDAC. That's why I don't think VSTM is simply another small biotech with a "promising molecule." There is a legitimate competitive efficacy signal here. And the mechanism makes sense This is another reason I am more confident. VS-7375 is designed to bind both: KRAS G12D ON and KRAS G12D OFF states.
$VSTM RAMP201 vs. Conventional Care

$VSTM 🕵️‍♂️But it gets even more interesting GenFleet's newer NSCLC Phase 2 data are substantially better than the original Phase 1 dataset. At 600 mg QD: 71 patients had at least one post-treatment assessment ... and: ORR = 59.2% confirmed ORR = 52.1% DCR = 93% That's a very serious signal in previously treated KRAS-G12D NSCLC. And the September update reported: median PFS = 9.6 months among taxane-naïve patients. The 12-month OS rate was 77% in the overall population. That is probably the single most important new piece of evidence for your question. And now look at the PDAC data This is where I think the VSTM story could become explosive.
